text: More than 650 years ago, the cities of Italy were among the richest places in Europe.
A poet named Petrarch hunted for the books of ancient writers and longed to bring back their wisdom.
src: In the 14th century the cities of northern and central Italy were among the richest and most literate places in Europe / years: 1340 to 1600
Francesco Petrarca, Petrarch / crowned poet laureate / He hunted for the works of Cicero / revive the language, literature and moral wisdom of ancient Rome and Greece

text: His followers, the humanists, studied grammar, poetry, history and how to live well, from the best ancient authors.
One humanist, Pico della Mirandola, wrote that humans are free to rise or fall by their own choice.
src: grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy, learned from the best Latin and, later, Greek authors / history and moral philosophy taught better than logic how to live
Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s Oration on the Dignity of Man / celebrated the human freedom to rise or fall by choice

text: Byzantine scholars came to Florence to teach Greek, so humanists could read Plato and Homer in the original.
Cosimo de' Medici, the master of Florence, paid for old books and for people to copy them.
src: in 1397 brought the Byzantine diplomat Manuel Chrysoloras to teach Greek / brought Byzantine scholars to Italy / learned Greek to read Plato, Homer and the Greek historians in the original
Cosimo de' Medici, master of Florence from 1434, paid for manuscripts and copyists

text: Humanists searched old monastery libraries and found lost books by ancient writers.
A pope, Nicholas V, gathered the books from which the Vatican Library grew.
src: Humanists hunted for lost manuscripts / searched monastery libraries north of the Alps
Pope Nicholas V, who commissioned Latin translations of the Greek historians and gathered the books from which the Vatican Library grew

text: Printing carried their ideas across Europe, where scholars such as Erasmus carried on their work.
Their way of teaching became the standard schooling of Europe for hundreds of years.
src: Carried across Europe by printing and by scholars such as Erasmus
The humanist school became the standard school of Europe / shaped European schooling for four centuries

text: In Venice, the printer Aldus Manutius printed the Greek classics and a new kind of letters called italic.
Even the letters in most printed books today come from the humanists' handwriting.
src: Aldus Manutius begins printing the Greek classics in Venice / from 1501 small portable classics in a new italic type
The roman type of most printed books today descends from a handwriting that Poggio Bracciolini and his Florentine circle developed
